name: Emerging / Frontier AI
intro:
Emerging and frontier AI is the catch-all for capabilities that don't fit established categories on this site because the products are new: computer-use and web agents like Anthropic's Computer Use and OpenAI's Operator lineage, an autonomous software engineer in Cognition's Devin, retrieval-optimized enterprise models from Cohere, a sovereign European model from Mistral, and embodied AI in humanoid robots from Figure AI, Physical Intelligence, and Tesla Optimus. It excludes mature chatbot products and settled categories elsewhere on the site, since what unites this group is that governance practice for each is still being written.

A buyer here isn't comparing products so much as which bet to place. Cohere and Mistral compete as enterprise-grade, sovereignty-conscious alternatives to the largest US labs. Devin and the Anthropic and OpenAI agents compete on autonomous task execution, software engineering versus general computer and browser control, each carrying credential risk traditional software never had. Figure AI, Physical Intelligence, and Tesla Optimus compete on getting a general-purpose humanoid robot into a real workplace first, a hardware and safety problem as much as a model one.

Capital and product moved together this year. Figure AI raised over $1 billion in a Series C at a $39 billion valuation in September 2025, and Physical Intelligence raised $600 million at $5.6 billion months later, signals that investors expect embodied AI to commercialize soon. ASML led a 1.7 billion euro round into Mistral in September 2025 at an 11.7 billion euro valuation, framed explicitly around European sovereign AI. OpenAI folded Operator into a broader ChatGPT agent in mid-2025, consolidating browsing and task execution into one product.

The clearest reference points are Figure AI and Physical Intelligence for embodied AI, given the capital behind them, and Devin as the sharpest test case for an agent with standing access to a codebase.

reading.body:
Frontier AI systems are shifting from text generation toward autonomous agents that control computers, robots, and physical infrastructure, creating safety and security risks that text-only models did not require.

The capability leap is qualitative. Earlier AI models answered questions. These systems make decisions and execute them: controlling browsers and desktops, writing and running code with full codebase access, operating humanoid robots in factories and homes, automating software engineering workflows. The risk profile changes fundamentally when an AI system can take actions in the world or in critical systems rather than merely proposing them. A language model's mistakes are bounded by a user's choice to act on them. An autonomous agent's mistakes execute immediately.

The concentration of these capabilities in US vendors is notable. Six of eight systems listed operate under US jurisdiction, with only Mistral Large 2 built explicitly for GDPR compliance and European sovereignty. This matters because autonomous agents operating across borders or handling European data face different regulatory pressure than text generation tools. The emergence of robots optimized for factory and household tasks adds a physical safety dimension that cloud-hosted models did not face.

The data does not cover deployment scale, energy consumption of these systems, the computational requirements for real-time autonomous operation, or how many data centers these agents will require. It also does not track incident rates or security breaches. What it shows is the category boundary itself: the frontier is no longer capability, but agency.
